children: F-Series is on track to be America's best-selling truck for a 50th consecutive year even after a serious supply disruption this year threatened the streak.

factories when fires at aluminum supplier Novelis' Oswego, New York, plant in September and November of last year wiped out roughly 40% of the U.S. sheet aluminum supply. The shortage starved F-150 production, and first-quarter F-Series sales fell 16% to 159,901 trucks, while Ram's sales jumped 25%. First-half F-Series sales declined 13.3% to 357,801. Ford's
CFO noted the company expects about $1.5 billion in Novelis-related costs for the full year.
Recovery for the F-Series came after the plant resumed operations in June. Ford

skipped summer shutdowns at four truck plants and added shifts. CEO Jim Farley has said the company is now fully recovered. By the third quarter, F-Series production rose 4.5% to 266,777 trucks, and Super Duty output hit a 19-year high. September F-Series sales rose 2.4% to 67,448. Through September, F-Series sales totaled 561,508, more than 140,000 ahead of the Chevrolet Silverado.

The F-Series traces its roots to 1948, when Ford introduced a line of trucks built on a dedicated truck platform rather than adapted from cars. It has been the top-selling U.S. truck every year since 1977, and it has also been the country's best-selling vehicle overall for most of the past four decades. The F-150 anchors the lineup, joined by the heavier-duty Super Duty trucks. The F-Series family is the profit engine of Ford's
North American business, with operating margins that have reached as high as 20%.
has not published 2027 F-Series sales targets, but the groundwork for a further rebound is visible, setting up the potential for a 51st year of topping the truck sales chart.
